opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it's one of the less glamorous parts of the work, and I think it's fair to be a bit critical of it. When people see a robot walking nicely in a video, they don't see the weeks of tweaking that went into the reward function behind it.

In practice, you start with the core objective, which is usually tracking a commanded velocity, and that alone almost never gives you something usable. The policy finds whatever works in simulation: it might drag its feet, vibrate, take tiny high-frequency steps, or exploit some quirk of the physics engine. So you add terms. You penalize joint torques and accelerations, you penalize action rate so the motions are smoother, you reward foot air time so it actually lifts its feet, you penalize collisions with the body, and so on. Before long you have fifteen or twenty terms, each with its own weight, and they interact in ways that aren't obvious.

So my judgment is that it works, and it's gotten us surprisingly far. With massively parallel simulation on GPUs, you can train a locomotion policy in minutes rather than days, and that makes the iteration loop fast enough that manual tuning is practical. You change a weight, retrain, look at the behavior, and adjust. That speed is a big part of why this approach became viable at all.

But it's also clearly a limitation. It doesn't scale well when you move from walking on flat ground to more complex skills: climbing, jumping, parkour-style behaviors, or manipulation combined with locomotion. Every new skill means another round of reward engineering, and a lot of the knowledge is in the heads of the people doing it rather than in any principled method. It's also fragile: a set of weights that works for one robot often doesn't transfer cleanly to another.

That's why I'm quite interested in ways to reduce that burden. Using motion data or demonstrations as a style prior, adversarial motion priors for example, can replace a lot of the hand-crafted "make it look natural" terms. Curriculum design and good domain randomization also matter as much as the reward itself. And longer term, I think we want approaches where you specify the task at a higher level and the system figures out the details, rather than an engineer hand-shaping every aspect of the gait.

So: effective, pragmatic, and a big reason legged robots work as well as they do today, but not something I'd consider a final solution.

r001.rationale: It describes adding many interacting reward terms to prevent undesirable behaviors and shape the desired gait, explaining why specifying walking behavior is complex.

r002.rationale: It judges manual tuning as effective and pragmatic, and says fast simulation makes it practical, while acknowledging its limitations.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I have a bit of a complicated relationship with, honestly. When we started with the ANYmal work and then later with the legged gym stuff on Isaac Gym, a huge fraction of the actual engineering time went into reward tuning. People see the final video of the robot walking over rough terrain and they imagine the learning did everything, but the reality is that there's a human sitting there for weeks going, okay, the robot is dragging its feet, let me add a foot clearance term, now it's hopping, let me penalize vertical velocity, now it's standing still because that's the safest thing to do, let me add an alive bonus or a tracking term and rebalance everything.

So on one hand I'd say it's a real weakness of the approach. It's not very principled. The rewards we ended up with in the papers, if you look at the config files, there are maybe ten or fifteen terms, and the weights look somewhat arbitrary because they are. They came out of trial and error. And it makes the results hard to reproduce for people coming into the field, because the paper says "we use a velocity tracking reward" and that hides a lot of the actual work. And it's also robot-specific, so when you move to a new platform you have to redo a good chunk of it.

On the other hand, I've come to see it as less of a problem than I used to. Part of why it felt so painful early on was that each iteration of the tuning loop took hours or days, because simulation was slow. Once training went down to minutes on a single GPU, the tuning loop became much more interactive. You change a weight, you watch the policy, you adjust. At that point reward design starts to feel a bit more like a design language for specifying behavior rather than a black art. You're encoding what you want the gait to look like, and that's actually information the engineer has and the learning algorithm doesn't.

So I'd put it this way: the tuning isn't the algorithm failing, it's us specifying the task. The thing that we should be honest about is that we usually don't know the task that precisely, so we're discovering it through the robot's failures. The directions I find more promising to reduce that burden are things like learning from motion references or demonstrations, where the style comes from data instead of hand-written terms, or using large models to propose and iterate on rewards. But even there, I think some amount of human judgment about what good locomotion looks like is going to stay in the loop for a while. I'd rather we make that part fast and transparent than pretend it doesn't exist.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes many reward terms as a way to encode the desired gait, and says tuning discovers what the task requires through failures.

r002.rationale: The candidate says reward tuning is task specification rather than an algorithmic failure, and accepts that human judgment will remain involved.

astra-6.text:
I think reward tuning is one of the more difficult parts of the process, because you have to describe what you want through a scalar reward. You can reward the robot for moving at a desired velocity, but that doesn’t tell it how you want it to walk. It might find a way of moving that achieves the objective but looks very unnatural, or uses excessive forces.

So you add terms for things like energy consumption and smoothness, and then you have to balance them. If you penalize energy too much, the robot might prefer to stand still. If you penalize it too little, it might learn a very aggressive gait. There’s quite a bit of iteration involved.

The way I look at it is that we haven’t eliminated the engineering effort; we’ve shifted some of it from designing the controller to designing the objective. The advantage is that we can let the policy discover the details of how to accomplish that objective.

r001.rationale: It explains that a velocity reward alone misses desired qualities such as naturalness and efficiency, so multiple terms must be added and balanced.

r002.rationale: It says reward design is difficult and shifts engineering effort to the objective, but does not clearly judge manual tuning of task requirements as acceptable.

sol-6.1.text:
I think reward tuning is one of the more challenging parts of learning locomotion. You can specify that the robot should follow a target velocity, but that doesn’t tell it how to walk. It might find a way to achieve that velocity that looks strange or puts a lot of stress on the hardware. So you add terms for things like energy consumption, smooth actions, and avoiding unwanted contacts.

The difficulty is balancing those terms. If you penalize energy too much, the robot may decide that standing still is a good solution. If you put too little weight on it, you can get very aggressive motions. It’s an iterative process: train a policy, look at what it does, and adjust the reward. There’s quite a bit of engineering judgment involved, and a reward that works for one robot doesn’t necessarily transfer directly to another.

r001.rationale: It explains that target velocity alone does not specify a desirable walk, so additional terms are needed for energy, smoothness, and contacts.

r002.rationale: It describes manual tuning as challenging and involving engineering judgment, but does not clearly judge that tuning task-related reward requirements to be acceptable.
